answer: Check the shoulders first: the shoulder seam should sit right at your shoulder bone. Then make sure the buttons lie flat across the chest or bust with 1–2 in to pinch at each side, long sleeves reach the wrist bone, and an untucked hem ends around the middle of your fly, covering the waistband but not your whole seat.
intro: This guide covers everyday button-up shirts: oxfords, flannels, chambray, linen and casual work shirts, for men and women. They're usually sized S–XL rather than by neck and sleeve, and they're often worn untucked, which makes length the most common problem. For formal shirts sized by collar, see the dress shirt guide.

checklist.good: The shoulder seam sits right at the edge of your shoulder bone.
checklist.tooTight: The seam rides up onto your shoulder and the back pulls tight when you reach forward.
checklist.tooLoose: The seam hangs down onto your upper arm, unless the shirt is cut with a deliberate dropped shoulder.

checklist.good: The buttons lie flat and you can pinch 1–2 in of fabric on each side of the chest.
checklist.tooTight: The placket gapes between buttons and pull lines point toward them.
checklist.tooLoose: The fabric balloons and hangs off the chest like a tent.

checklist.good: The sleeve follows your arm with a little room, and you can lift your arms without the hem rising more than an inch or two.
checklist.tooTight: The sleeve clings to your biceps and the armhole cuts in when you reach.
checklist.tooLoose: The sleeve flaps around your arm and the armhole drops several inches below the armpit.

checklist.good: Long sleeves end at the wrist bone or base of the thumb; short sleeves end around mid-biceps.
checklist.tooTight: Too short: the cuff lands above the wrist bone, or short sleeves ride up near the shoulder.
checklist.tooLoose: Too long: the cuff covers your hand, or short sleeves reach down toward the elbow.

checklist.good: The shirt falls straight or tapers slightly over your stomach without clinging.
checklist.tooTight: Buttons strain at the stomach and the fabric creases horizontally when you sit.
checklist.tooLoose: Extra fabric billows at the sides and the shirt looks boxy untucked.

checklist.good: Untucked, the hem ends around the middle of your fly; tucked, the tails stay in when you raise your arms.
checklist.tooTight: Too short: your waistband or stomach shows when you lift your arms.
checklist.tooLoose: Too long: an untucked hem covers your entire seat and makes your legs look short.

variations.heading: Fit by style and wearer
variations.intro: Casual shirts come in many cuts. Start with the shoulders, then judge the rest against the style.

items.name: Untucked casual shirts
items.text: Look for a straight hem or a shallow curve that ends at mid-fly. Many brands sell an untucked line cut 1–2 in shorter than a standard shirt.

items.name: Tucked shirts and oxfords
items.text: Need longer tails that reach mid-seat so they stay tucked. A deeply curved shirttail hem is designed for tucking; worn out, it can look too long.

items.name: Flannels and overshirts
items.text: Cut roomier so they can be worn open over a T-shirt or layered under a jacket. Allow more ease in the chest and sleeves, but the shoulder seam should still land near your shoulder bone.

items.name: Short-sleeve shirts
items.text: The sleeve should end around the middle of your biceps and leave about a finger's width of space between fabric and arm. Camp-collar shirts are meant to be boxier, with a straight hem for wearing out.

items.name: Women's button-up shirts
items.text: Check the bust first: the front should stay closed when you raise your arms or sit. Shaping with darts or princess seams helps. Oversized or boyfriend shirts are cut loose, with dropped shoulders and longer hems, and can be tucked at the front or knotted.

items.name: Big and tall
items.text: Tall sizes add body and sleeve length, typically an inch or two; big sizes add width without extra length. Choose by what's missing rather than just going up a size.

measure.heading: How to find your shirt size
measure.intro: Casual shirts are usually sized S–XXL or by women's numeric sizes. Letter sizes vary a lot between brands, so compare your measurements with each chart.
steps: Measure around the fullest part of your chest or bust, under the armpits, keeping the tape level.
Measure your waist at the navel for men's shirts or at the narrowest point for women's.
Measure from the center back of your neck, over the shoulder, to the wrist bone for sleeve length.
Lay a shirt you like flat and measure across the chest from armpit to armpit and from the base of the collar to the hem at the back.
Compare these with the brand's garment measurements; most online shops list chest width and body length.
measure.tip: Cotton shirts, especially flannel and untreated cotton, can shrink a little in length after washing in hot water or drying on high heat. Wash cool and line dry if the fit is already close.

problems.problem: Shirt is too long to wear untucked
problems.fix: Look for shirts labeled untucked or short-length, or have a tailor shorten the hem. It's a simple alteration for a straight hem.

problems.problem: Buttons gape at the chest or bust
problems.fix: Size up and have the waist taken in, choose a shirt with a hidden snap or button, or pick a stretch fabric.

problems.problem: Shoulders fit but the body is baggy
problems.fix: Try a slim fit in the same size, or have a tailor add darts at the back and take in the side seams.
Roll them for casual wear, or have a tailor shorten them at the cuff.
Low armholes make the whole shirt lift when you raise your arms. Try a slimmer cut, since armholes are hard to alter.

extra.heading: Casual shirt vs dress shirt fit
extra.body: A dress shirt is sized by neck and sleeve, cut with long tails for tucking and fitted at the collar for a tie. A casual shirt is usually sized S–XL, may have a button-down or camp collar, and is often cut shorter to wear untucked. Judging a casual shirt by dress shirt rules leads to choosing one that's too long; judging a dress shirt by casual rules leads to one that won't stay tucked.

picks.label: Shirts cut for wearing untucked
picks.why: Shorter, straighter hems end at mid-fly without alteration.

picks.label: Stretch oxford or poplin shirts
picks.why: A little stretch helps the buttons stay closed across the chest or bust when you move.

picks.label: Women's button-up shirts with hidden buttons
picks.why: A concealed button or snap at the bust keeps the placket from gaping.

faqs.q: How should a shirt fit a woman?
faqs.a: The shoulder seam should sit at your shoulder bone, the front should close flat across the bust with no gaping between buttons, and the sleeves should reach your wrist. Oversized styles are loose on purpose but still shouldn't slip off the shoulder.

faqs.q: How should a shirt fit a man?
faqs.a: Shoulder seams at the shoulder bones, 1–2 in to pinch at the chest, sleeves at the wrist bone and, untucked, a hem around mid-fly.

faqs.q: How long should a shirt be untucked?
faqs.a: The hem should end around the middle of your zipper fly, covering your waistband when you stand but not hiding your entire seat.
Around the middle of your biceps, with roughly a finger's width of space between the sleeve and your arm.

faqs.q: Should a shirt be tight or loose?
faqs.a: Somewhere between: close enough to follow your shape, loose enough to pinch 1–2 in at each side of the chest and move freely without the buttons pulling.

faqs.q: How do I know if my shirt is too big?
faqs.a: The shoulder seam drops down your arm, you can pinch more than 2 in at the chest, and the fabric billows at the waist. If only the body is loose, a tailor can take it in.
